name: Norway
traditionNote: A Nordic system that resists the usual labels: statutes are central and codification is partial, the Høyesterett's reasoning binds later courts in practice if not in form, and unwritten law developed by the courts — in contract, tort and administrative law — carries real weight alongside the enacted text.
summary: Acts (lov) are passed by the Storting, which since 2009 has been a single chamber, sanctioned by the King in Council and published in Norsk Lovtidend. Regulations (forskrift) are made by the King, a ministry or a delegated body under an authorisation in an act, and are published in the same series — as are local regulations made by municipalities and county authorities, which is unusual: Norwegian municipal rules go into the national gazette rather than only into a local one. Norsk Lovtidend has been published electronically since 2001, by Lovdata, a private foundation set up by the Ministry of Justice and the University of Oslo's law faculty and charged with the publication; the electronic version is the authoritative one. Norway is not an EU member but is inside the internal market through the EEA Agreement, so a large body of EU legislation applies after being incorporated by the EEA Joint Committee and implemented domestically. There is no constitutional court: the Høyesterett reviews statutes against the Grunnloven in the course of ordinary cases, a power it asserted for itself in the nineteenth century and which was written into Article 89 in 2015.
hierarchy: Kongeriket Norges Grunnlov (Constitution of 17 May 1814), the second-oldest written constitution still in force
Incorporated human rights conventions — the ECHR and the UN covenants — which under the Human Rights Act prevail over other statutes
EEA law as incorporated and implemented, with the EEA Act giving implemented EEA rules precedence over conflicting statutory provisions
Lov — acts of the Storting, and plenary decisions of the Storting such as the annual tax resolutions
Forskrift — regulations of the King in Council, ministries and delegated bodies
Lokale forskrifter — local regulations of counties and municipalities, published in Norsk Lovtidend
Enkeltvedtak and administrative practice — individual decisions and the internal instructions behind them

gazette.name: Norsk Lovtidend
gazette.authority: Justis- og beredskapsdepartementet; published by Stiftelsen Lovdata under statutory mandate
gazette.coverage: Division I for acts and central regulations and Division II for local regulations; electronic publication since 2001, with the printed series before that
gazette.desc: The gazette in which Norwegian acts and regulations are promulgated. It is published by a private foundation rather than by a ministry directly — an arrangement peculiar to Norway — and the electronic issue on Lovdata is the authoritative one. Every item carries the date it was published, which is what the rules on entry into force run from.
gazette.howto: Browse the register by year and by division: Avdeling I for acts and central regulations, Avdeling II for local ones. New items appear as they are promulgated and can be followed by RSS. From a consolidated act, the Lovtidend item behind each amendment is linked from the amendment note.
gazette.note: Publication in Lovtidend is a condition of a regulation being applied against a citizen — an unpublished regulation generally cannot be invoked to their detriment.

constitution.name: Grunnloven
constitution.en: The Constitution of the Kingdom of Norway
constitution.authority: Riksforsamlingen at Eidsvoll, 17 May 1814; maintained in consolidated form by Lovdata
constitution.coverage: In force since 1814 and amended continuously since, with a full linguistic revision in 2014 and the addition of a human rights chapter in the same year
constitution.desc: The oldest constitution in Europe still in force and the second oldest in the world. It was rewritten in modern Norwegian in 2014 without changing its substance, and given a catalogue of human rights in the same revision; judicial review of statutes, exercised by the courts since the 1800s, was codified in Article 89 in 2015.
constitution.howto: Read the consolidated text on Lovdata, which shows the amendments in place; an English version is published at lovdata.no/dokument/NLE/lov/1814-05-17. Amendment proposals must be tabled in one Storting and voted in the next, so a proposal and its adoption are years apart.
constitution.note: Amendment requires two-thirds of the Storting after an intervening general election, and the amendment must not contradict the Constitution's principles — a limit that has never been enforced by a court.

sources.name: Lover (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Stiftelsen Lovdata, on behalf of the Ministry of Justice and Public Security
sources.coverage: All acts in force, consolidated with their amendments, each identified as LOV-year-month-day-number
sources.desc: The consolidated text of Norwegian statute law, free on the open side of Lovdata. Each act shows the amendments incorporated with a note naming the amending act, and the chronological identifier makes a citation unambiguous without a title.
sources.howto: Browse the register alphabetically or by date, or search; open an act and use the paragraph links, since Norwegian citation is by section (§) rather than by page. The 'Endringer' notes at the foot of a provision name the amending act and its date of entry into force.
sources.note: The free service holds acts and regulations in force. Repealed acts, older versions and much of the case law are on the subscription side, Lovdata Pro.

sources.name: Sentrale forskrifter (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Stiftelsen Lovdata; regulations made by the King in Council, ministries and delegated bodies
sources.coverage: Central regulations in force, consolidated, identified as FOR-year-month-day-number
sources.desc: Where most of the operative detail of Norwegian law sits. An act typically sets the frame and delegates the substance to a forskrift, so the rule that decides a case is more often a regulation than a statute.
sources.howto: Search or browse by issuing ministry; each regulation names the statutory provision it is made under, which is the check on whether it is validly made at all. Local regulations are in a separate register.
sources.note: A regulation that goes beyond its enabling provision is invalid, and Norwegian courts do set them aside — the authorising section at the head of the text is worth reading first.

sources.name: Lokale forskrifter (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Municipalities and county authorities; published in Norsk Lovtidend by Lovdata
sources.coverage: Local regulations in force, arranged by county and municipality
sources.desc: Norway publishes municipal regulations nationally, which few states do: parking rules, water and sewerage charges, hunting and motor-traffic rules in the outfields, school catchment rules, all in the same gazette as an act of the Storting and searchable in the same place.
sources.howto: Pick the county and then the municipality, or search by subject; each regulation cites the act it is made under and the date it was published in Lovtidend.
sources.note: Individual decisions of a municipality — a building permit, a refusal of a service — are not regulations and are not here; those follow the appeal route in the Public Administration Act.

sources.name: Rettsavgjorelser (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Stiftelsen Lovdata, publishing decisions supplied by the courts
sources.coverage: Supreme Court decisions from 2000 onward and selected appeal and district court decisions on the free side; the full historical collection, including Norsk Retstidend, on Lovdata Pro
sources.desc: The route to Norwegian case law. Since 2016 Supreme Court decisions are cited as HR-2016-1234-A rather than by Rt. page number, and the letter at the end says which formation decided it — A for a chamber, P for the plenary, S for the grand chamber.
sources.howto: Search by case identifier, date or keyword; the free collection is enough for recent Supreme Court practice, and the subscription side is where older material and the bulk of lower-court decisions live. The Høyesterett's own site lists its decisions by year with summaries.
sources.note: The division between the free and paid sides of Lovdata is the main practical limit on free access to Norwegian law, and it falls mostly on case law rather than on legislation.

sources.name: Hoyesterett
sources.coverage: Decisions by year with summaries, the hearing schedule, and summaries of selected judgments in English
sources.desc: The final instance in all types of case — civil, criminal and administrative — and the body that exercises constitutional review in the course of deciding them. Norway has no separate constitutional or administrative supreme court.
sources.howto: Take 'Avgjørelser' and the year for the list of decisions with short summaries, then follow into the full text on Lovdata. The court's English pages carry summaries of decisions of international interest.
sources.note: Leave to appeal is decided by the Appeals Selection Committee and is given in a small minority of cases; its refusals are decisions too, and are published.

sources.name: Stortinget — saker og publikasjoner
sources.coverage: Bills (proposisjoner), committee recommendations (innstillinger), representative proposals, questions and the full record of debates, by session
sources.desc: Where a Norwegian act is followed and where its preparatory works are. Norwegian interpretation leans hard on forarbeider: the ministry's proposition, the committee's innstilling and the debate are read as evidence of what a provision means, and the NOU reports behind them go further back still.
sources.howto: Search by case, document type or session; a bill's page shows every document in the file and the votes. The open data service at data.stortinget.no exposes the same material for scripted work.
sources.note: Green and white papers (NOU and meldinger) are published by the Government on regjeringen.no rather than here; that site answers automated requests with 403.

sources.name: Norges traktater (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Utenriksdepartementet (Ministry of Foreign Affairs); published through Lovdata
sources.coverage: Treaties binding on Norway, with their status and the domestic instruments relating to them
sources.desc: Norway is dualist, so a treaty binds the state internationally without becoming internal law; it applies domestically only through incorporation or transformation. The exception is large: the human rights conventions incorporated by the Human Rights Act take precedence over ordinary statutes.
sources.howto: Search the treaty register by title, party or date, then look for the Norwegian act or regulation that gives it internal effect. The EEA Agreement has a register of its own on the same site.

sources.name: EOS-avtalen (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Stiftelsen Lovdata, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
sources.coverage: The EEA Agreement with its annexes and protocols, and the EU acts incorporated into them
sources.desc: The mechanism by which most EU legislation reaches Norway. An EU act is taken into an annex of the Agreement by the EEA Joint Committee, then implemented by Norwegian act or regulation; the EEA Act gives implemented EEA rules precedence over conflicting Norwegian statutory provisions.
sources.howto: Work from the annex covering the field to the incorporated act, then to the Norwegian implementing regulation. Europalov.no tracks the pipeline from Brussels through the Joint Committee to Norwegian implementation, which is the part that is hard to see otherwise.
sources.note: Norway is not an EU member and EU regulations do not apply of their own force; there is always a Norwegian instrument, and finding it is part of the work. The EFTA Court, not the Court of Justice, gives advisory opinions on EEA law for Norway.

sources.name: Translated acts (Lovdata)
sources.authority: Stiftelsen Lovdata, gathering translations produced by ministries
sources.coverage: A selection of acts and regulations in English, and English summaries of selected decisions; coverage is uneven and weighted to business and maritime law
sources.desc: The state's collected English versions of Norwegian legislation. Norway translates more maritime, petroleum and company law than most, because those fields are transacted internationally, and comparatively little else.
sources.howto: Browse the register of translated acts, and the parallel registers for regulations and decisions; check the date on the translation, since some are frozen at the version current when they were made.
sources.note: Translations are unofficial. Only the Norwegian text has legal force, and the two written standards of Norwegian — bokmål and nynorsk — are both official for that purpose.

sources.name: Lovdata Pro
sources.coverage: The complete collection: historical versions of acts and regulations, repealed law, the full case-law archive including Norsk Retstidend, preparatory works, journals and annotations
sources.desc: The same foundation's paid service, and the reason Norwegian free access looks generous for legislation and thin for case law. Practitioners work here; the open side is what everyone else gets.
sources.howto: Access requires a subscription; students and members of some professions have institutional access. For a historical version of a statute without a subscription, the amendment notes on the free text plus the Lovtidend items behind them will reconstruct it.
sources.note: Lovdata is a private foundation with a public mandate — official for what it publishes as the gazette, commercial in what it sells on top.

sources.name: Regjeringen.no
sources.en: Government documents, NOU and white papers
sources.coverage: Official inquiry reports (NOU), white papers (meldinger), consultation documents (høringer) and circulars, by ministry and year
sources.desc: The stage before a bill. Norwegian legislation typically starts with an expert committee's NOU, goes out to consultation, and only then becomes a proposition to the Storting — and all three layers are cited as preparatory works when the resulting provision is interpreted.
sources.howto: Filter documents by type and ministry; a consultation page lists every response received, which is often the clearest account of what the affected sectors thought a rule would do.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Sivilombudet
sources.en: Parliamentary Ombud for Scrutiny of Public Administration
sources.coverage: Published statements on complaints against the administration, and the reports of its national preventive mechanism on places of detention
sources.desc: The main published commentary on Norwegian administrative law: how discretion may be exercised, what reasons a decision must give, when access to documents can be refused. Its statements are followed by the administration as a matter of course.
sources.howto: Search the statements by subject or authority; each states the case, the provisions and the conclusion. Where the Ombud finds an error, the follow-up is usually recorded too.
sources.note: The Ombud cannot annul a decision or award compensation; it states an opinion, which the administration is expected to act on.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an act
findLaw.steps: Search or browse the acts register on Lovdata and open the consolidated text; cite by section, as in § 15 of the act, and note the LOV identifier with its date and number. The amendment notes under each provision name the act that gave it its current wording.

findLaw.task: Find the regulation under an act
findLaw.steps: Most of the detail is in a forskrift, not in the act. Search the central regulations register, or work from the act's enabling provision — every regulation states the section it is made under at the head of its text. Local rules are in the separate register of local regulations.

Open Norsk Lovtidend and find the item by year and division — Avdeling I for acts and central regulations, Avdeling II for local ones. This is also how you establish the publication date, which the rules on entry into force and on enforceability against citizens run from.

Search the decisions register by identifier — HR-2016-1234-A for decisions from 2016 onward, Rt. year and page for older ones — or browse the Court's own year lists with their summaries. Recent Supreme Court practice is on the free side of Lovdata; the older archive is behind the subscription.

findLaw.task: Work out what a provision was meant to mean
findLaw.steps: Follow the preparatory works: the proposition to the Storting and the committee's innstilling on the Storting site, and behind them the NOU report and the consultation on regjeringen.no. Norwegian courts treat these as evidence of meaning, so they are part of the answer rather than background to it.

findLaw.task: Find the EU rule that applies in Norway
findLaw.steps: Norway is in the EEA, not the EU, so an EU act applies only once incorporated into an annex of the EEA Agreement and implemented domestically. Start from the EEA register to find the incorporating decision, then find the Norwegian act or regulation that implements it — that instrument, not the EU act, is what binds.

findLaw.task: Read a Norwegian act in English
findLaw.steps: Check the register of translated acts, which is strongest on maritime, petroleum, company and procedural law. If the act you need is not there, no official English version exists; the Constitution is one of the few texts with a maintained English edition.

subnational: Norway is a unitary state with two levels below the centre — counties and municipalities — and neither legislates in the sense of enacting statutes. What they make are lokale forskrifter under powers delegated by act, together with budgets, plans and individual decisions. The distinctive feature is publication: local regulations go into Norsk Lovtidend, division II, and are searchable in the national database by county and municipality, so Norwegian local law is far easier to find than local law in most states. Svalbard is governed under the Svalbard Act with a Governor appointed by the state and a local council with limited powers, and Norwegian law applies there only where a statute says so — a rule that catches out anyone assuming the mainland corpus extends automatically. The Sámi Parliament is an elected representative body with consultation rights and administrative functions rather than legislative power; the rules on reindeer husbandry and on Sámi language rights are national acts.
caveats: Norway's free legal information is generous for legislation and restricted for case law: Lovdata's open side carries acts, regulations and recent Supreme Court decisions, while the historical archive, repealed law, older versions and the bulk of lower-court judgments are behind the Lovdata Pro subscription. Lovdata is a private foundation acting under a public mandate, which is unusual and worth stating plainly — official as publisher of Lovtidend, commercial in what it sells beside it. Because so much operative law is in regulations, an act read alone is often misleading, and a regulation that exceeds its enabling provision is invalid, so the authority note at its head matters. EEA law does not apply of its own force: there is always a Norwegian instrument, and looking only at the EU act will not tell you what applies in Norway or from when. Translations are unofficial and selective. Finally, both bokmål and nynorsk are official written standards, and a statute exists in the one it was passed in.
